intro: VialGrade is a research site that brings together lab records and other evidence about peptide vendors. I built it because I wanted a better way to compare them than just taking a website's word for it.
orientation: The site cross-checks lab records and batch information, then shows what it can support and what it still doesn't know.
origin: A friend of mine is really into biomedicine and peptide research. He told me a lot of people around him wanted to buy peptides, but the vendors seemed sketchy. When I started looking, that was basically my reaction too. Every site seemed to have third-party testing and purity numbers, but it was hard to tell what any of that actually proved.

So I thought, why can't I use AI and software to cross-check the claims? A certificate of analysis, or COA, is a lab report. I wanted to check whether its details matched the batch and company being named, rather than just see that a vendor had uploaded a document.
unknown: One thing I had to be careful with was how to handle missing information. Not finding a lab record isn't the same as finding something wrong with a vendor. I didn't want a lack of data to turn into a bad grade, so VialGrade can leave a vendor ungraded when there isn't enough to go on.
grading: The grade also looks beyond a single certificate. It considers independent testing alongside regulatory records and information about the business. A documented problem still matters even when other records look good, and a high grade doesn't tell you that a product is safe to use.
handoff: I originally wanted checkout on VialGrade, but I couldn't make that work, so the site links to the vendor's page instead. That created another problem: once someone left, I couldn't see what happened next.
attribution: I added tracking tags and a short VialGrade click reference to the links. That lets me track clicks out of the site and identify where the traffic came from, but a click still doesn't tell me that someone bought anything.
earlyUse: In an early update, I'd recorded about 2,000 Google impressions, around 600 clicks into the site, and eight signups over a month. That honestly surprised me. It was still small, but people finding something I'd built made it feel a lot more real.
takeaway: The hardest part wasn't putting a letter next to a vendor. It was deciding when the evidence actually justified one. I wanted the site to make that difference easy to see, including when I didn't have enough information yet.
